The aims of my thesis were (1) to investigate the efficacy of existing multi- component ex ercise- based injury prevention programmes (IPPs); (2) to describe the development process for the first IPP specifically designed for youth football players, called ‘FUNBALL ’; (3) to evaluate the efficacy of ‘FUNBALL ’ and (4) to describe the epidemiology of injuries that occurred in the control arm of study 3. WHY DID I DO IT? Injury prevention in football is essential for main- taining long- term engagement in the sport. Several meta- analyses support the efficacy of exercise- based IPP to reduce the risk of football- related injuries by up to 51%. 1–3 However, their methodological quality and the certainty of the findings are ques- tionable. 4 Furthermore, adherence to and mainte- nance of IPPs is challenging, which may be due to a lack of football- specific exercises and/or player enjoyment.5 HOW DID I DO IT? A total of four articles were included in the thesis. This systematic review reported incidence rate ratios (IRRs) with predic- tion intervals (PIs) in addition to 95% CIs. This approach is widely recommended for interpreting results from a random- effects meta- analysis of trials assessing treatment effects.4 7 My second study 8 was a viewpoint article. My third study 12 included a large- scale cluster - randomised controlled trial that investigated the efficacy of the ‘FUNBALL ’ programme in male youth football players. A total of 1027 players from Kosovo who were competing in the Under (U) 15, U17 and U19 age groups were randomised either into the intervention or control group. The intervention group (n=524 players) performed the 15–20 min ‘FUNBALL ’ programme in addition to their usual training at least two times per week, whereas the control group (n=503 players) continued their regular training routine. Both groups were followed for one football season (August 2021–May 2022). My fourth study 13 was a secondary analysis of the data collected in the second study, which evaluated the epidemiology of football- related injuries in players of the control arm who were not exposed to the ‘FUNBALL ’ programme. WHAT DID I FIND? My first study indicated that the treatment effect associated with the use of multi- component ex ercise- based IPPs in football is uncertain and inconclusive (figure 1). This conclusion was based on the observation that the PI values crossed ‘1’, which marks the programme’s cut- off point for being either protective (<1) or indicative of increased injury risk (>1). Also, the results were mainly based on very low and low quality of evidence. According to my third study, the ‘FUNBALL ’ programme reduced the incidence rate for the overall number of time- loss injuries by 31% (IRR 0.69, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.87, p=0.002) when it was implemented for one football season. Thigh injury incidence was reduced by 38% (IRR 0.62, 95% CI 0.39 to 0.98, p=0.042); moderate injuries (time- loss between 7 and 28 days) were reduced by 35% (IRR 0.65, 95% CI 0.44 to 0.97, p=0.035) and severe injuries (time- loss >28 days) were reduced by 49% (IRR 0.51, 95% CI 0.28 to 0.91, p=0.024). Injury burden was nearly halved in the intervention group (40 vs 74 days lost per 1000 hours). The key finding from my fourth study was a lower injury incidence in youth players compared with adult players. The most commonly injured body regions (thigh, knee and ankle) comprised 64% of all injuries in the male players aged 13–19 years. We observed a higher injury incidence in the older age groups. No commercial re- use . See rights and permissions. Published by BMJ Group. WHAT DID I DO? The aims of my thesis were (1) to investigate the efficacy of existing multi- component ex ercise- based injury prevention programmes (IPPs); (2) to describe the development process for the first IPP specifically designed for youth football players, called ‘FUNBALL ’; (3) to evaluate the efficacy of ‘FUNBALL ’ and (4) to describe the epidemiology of injuries that occurred in the control arm of study 3. WHY DID I DO IT? Injury prevention in football is essential for main- taining long- term engagement in the sport. Several meta- analyses support the efficacy of exercise- based IPP to reduce the risk of football- related injuries by up to 51%. 1–3 However, their methodological quality and the certainty of the findings are ques- tionable. 4 Furthermore, adherence to and mainte- nance of IPPs is challenging, which may be due to a lack of football- specific exercises and/or player enjoyment.5 HOW DID I DO IT? A total of four articles were included in the thesis. My first study (a systematic review and meta- analysis)6 examined the efficacy of multi- component exercise- based IPP s on reducing football- related injuries among footballers of all age groups. 15 studies (n=22 177 players) were included in the analysis. This systematic review reported incidence rate ratios (IRRs) with predic- tion intervals (PIs) in addition to 95% CIs. This approach is widely recommended for interpreting results from a random- effects meta- analysis of trials assessing treatment effects.4 7 My second study 8 was a viewpoint article. It described the developmental process of the ‘FUNBALL ’ programme, including the rationale, end- user involvement (eg, coach and football feder- ation administrators) and the iterative design and piloting steps. The ‘FUNBALL ’ programme was developed specifically for youth (aged 13–19 years) footballers with end- users, to be used after the usual warm- up. It aimed to address known implementa - tion barriers, such as a lack of football relevance, time and player/coach enjoyment. 9 This is achieved through the inclusion of ‘FUN’ activities to better address the barrier of player and coach engagement, particularly for youth age groups. The ‘FUNBALL ’ programme includes six mandatory exercise cate- gories and one optional category of games. Exer - cise categories were evidence- based,10 and each included two different exercises, which coaches were free to choose. All exercises were organised into progressive levels of difficulty. The ‘FUNBALL ’ programme incorporated exercises that allow for competition between players. My third study 12 included a large- scale cluster - randomised controlled trial that investigated the efficacy of the ‘FUNBALL ’ programme in male youth football players. A total of 1027 players from Kosovo who were competing in the Under (U) 15, U17 and U19 age groups were randomised either into the intervention or control group. The intervention group (n=524 players) performed the 15–20 min ‘FUNBALL ’ programme in addition to their usual training at least two times per week, whereas the control group (n=503 players) continued their regular training routine. Both groups were followed for one football season (August 2021–May 2022). My fourth study 13 was a secondary analysis of the data collected in the second study, which evaluated the epidemiology of football- related injuries in players of the control arm who were not exposed to the ‘FUNBALL ’ programme. WHAT DID I FIND? My first study indicated that the treatment effect associated with the use of multi- component ex ercise- based IPPs in football is uncertain and inconclusive (figure 1). This conclusion was based on the observation that the PI values crossed ‘1’, which marks the programme’s cut- off point for being either protective (<1) or indicative of increased injury risk (>1). Also, the results were mainly based on very low and low quality of evidence. According to my third study, the ‘FUNBALL ’ programme reduced the incidence rate for the overall number of time- loss injuries by 31% (IRR 0.69, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.87, p=0.002) when it was implemented for one football season. Thigh injury incidence was reduced by 38% (IRR 0.62, 95% CI 0.39 to 0.98, p=0.042); moderate injuries (time- loss between 7 and 28 days) were reduced by 35% (IRR 0.65, 95% CI 0.44 to 0.97, p=0.035) and severe injuries (time- loss >28 days) were reduced by 49% (IRR 0.51, 95% CI 0.28 to 0.91, p=0.024). Injury burden was nearly halved in the intervention group (40 vs 74 days lost per 1000 hours). The key finding from my fourth study was a lower injury incidence in youth players compared with adult players. The most commonly injured body regions (thigh, knee and ankle) comprised 64% of all injuries in the male players aged 13–19 years. We observed a higher injury incidence in the older age groups. WHAT IS THE MOST IMPORTANT PRACTICAL FINDING? Based on the third study, the ‘FUNBALL ’ programme reduced overall time- loss injury incidence in male youth football players and was most effective for thigh injuries. The programme contained more football- specific elements compared with existing IPPs, which may increase implementation of the ‘FUNBALL ’ programme.
